fprintf("center of mass - center of figure = [%.2f %.2f %.2f] m\n", 1e3*(fm.com_km - body.centroid_km))
fprintf("Izz / (M R_ref^2) = %.4f\n", fm.inertia_norm(3))

The core is centered at the shape-model origin, 57 m from the center of figure, so the center of mass moves toward it and the degree-1 coefficients about the center of figure are not zero.

Measurements and inversion

Measurement sets#

A measurement set (obs) holds fully normalized gravity coefficients with their covariance, moment-of-inertia measurement rows, the total mass, the reference radius and the expansion origin.

Sources#

Source Function Notes
A simulated interior sbtk.data.simulate Exact values about the true center of mass, without uncertainties (they are NaN until set, below); coef_about = 'origin'.
An SBTK measurement package sbtk.exchange.read_data Coefficients about the measured center of mass with their full covariance; returns the body as well (Exchange packages).
A gravity file in the PDS SHADR layout sbtk.exchange.read_shadr Header row (R, GM, σGM, degree, order, normalization state, …) then rows l, m, C, S, sigma_C, sigma_S; diagonal covariance. The caller gives the shape model and the point the coefficients are about.
A JPL SSD gravity file sbtk.io.read_jpl_gravity MATLAB-assignment form with NAMES, VALS, COV; parsed as text; full covariance; Jl converted to C¯l0.
Coefficient matrices sbtk.data.from_coefficients C(l+1, m+1), S(l+1, m+1) and their 1σ; diagonal covariance.
The SBTK text format sbtk.io.read_measurements, sbtk.io.load_measurements One keyword per line; diagonal covariance only (Results folders).

Uncertainties and covariance#

  • Exact values have none. sbtk.data.simulate returns the true model's exact values without uncertainties: coef_cov and every inertia σ are NaN. Measurements need them: sbtk.data.add_noise, sbtk.invert.setup and sbtk.exchange.write_data stop with sbtk:data:noUncertainties otherwise.
  • By degree. sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(obs, unc) gives every coefficient of degree l the 1σ of sbtk.data.uncertainties for that degree (a diagonal covariance), every inertia element its 1σ (as a fraction of MRref2), and the libration row the 1σ of the ratio times Izz/(MRref2).
  • From another data set. sbtk.data.use_uncertainties gives every coefficient that a reference data set also contains the reference's variances and covariances, converted to the reference radius of the target by (R/R′)l. Coefficients the reference lacks keep their variances and become uncorrelated with the others.
  • Full covariance. sbtk.data.set_covariance replaces the coefficient covariance with any symmetric positive definite matrix in the order of obs.coef_labels.
  • Inertia rows. sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma sets the σ of named rows; the field libration gives the 1σ of the ratio.

Noise#

sbtk.data.add_noise(obs, seed) returns one realization: the coefficients plus L𝐳, with L the lower Cholesky factor of the coefficient covariance and 𝐳 standard normal; each inertia row plus its σ times a standard normal variable. The same seed gives the same noise; obs.noise_seed records it.

Inertia measurements and the center of mass#

Function Adds
sbtk.data.add_moi One element Ixx … Iyz as I/(MRref2) (sbtk.units.moi_to_norm converts from kg m²).
sbtk.data.add_moi_row Any linear combination of the six elements.
sbtk.data.add_libration The libration ratio (B−A)/C as a linear row (Moments of inertia). Requires C¯22 and S¯22.
sbtk.data.libration_ratio_from_amplitude Computes the ratio and its 1σ from a forced libration amplitude.
sbtk.data.add_center_of_mass The measured center of mass as degree-1 coefficients; sets coef_about to 'center_of_mass'.

Selecting measurements#

sbtk.data.select_degree keeps the coefficients up to a degree, sbtk.data.select_coefficients a list of coefficients, and sbtk.data.select_moi a list of inertia rows; the covariance keeps the matching rows and columns. sbtk.data.move_origin changes the expansion origin of data about the center of mass. sbtk.data.summary prints the contents of a measurement set.

Example#

MATLAB script: Measurements from coefficient matrices
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Dimorphos", sbtk.shape.bundled("dimorphos"), 2.700e9, 0.10);

% coefficient matrices, C(l+1, m+1) = C_lm, fully normalized, about the shape-model origin
L = 2;
C = zeros(L + 1);  S = zeros(L + 1);
C(1,1) = 1;  C(3,1) = -0.08;  C(3,3) = 0.03;  S(3,3) = 0.002;     % C00, C20, C22, S22
Cs = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);  Ss = 1e-3*ones(L + 1);                     % 1-sigma of each
obs = sbtk.data.from_coefficients(body, "example", [0 0 0], C, S, Cs, Ss);

% a polar moment given in kg m^2, and a libration ratio
Izz = sbtk.units.moi_to_norm(1.6e14, body.mass_kg, body.R_ref_km);
obs = sbtk.data.add_moi(obs, "Izz", Izz, 0.01*Izz);
obs = sbtk.data.add_libration(obs, 0.20, 0.03, Izz);

% 30% correlation between all coefficients
sig = sqrt(diag(obs.coef_cov));
obs = sbtk.data.set_covariance(obs, (0.3 + 0.7*eye(numel(sig))).*(sig*sig'));
sbtk.data.summary(obs)

Calculations has further examples: simulated data with uncertainties from another data set, selection of inertia rows, and reading files.

Measurements and inversion

Density estimation#

The inversion estimates the background density and the relative densities of a set of components from a measurement set, and optionally parts of their geometry: the position of spheres, ellipsoids and tori and the axis of ellipsoids and tori (Estimated geometry).

Procedure#

sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, opts) builds the geometry about obs.origin_km and the design matrix once (prob); sbtk.invert.run(prob) solves. sbtk.invert.solve does both. Reusing prob is faster when the same problem is solved more than once:

  • with other settings that do not select measurements (prob.opts.regularization, bounds, positions);
  • for a homogeneous body (sbtk.invert.homogeneous);
  • for other realizations of the same measurements (sbtk.invert.replace_data).

Estimation problem#

Let 𝐲 be the n measurements (the selected coefficients followed by the inertia rows named in opts.moi_labels) with covariance Σ=LL𝖳. The predictions are linear in the densities:

𝐲pred=ρbg𝐠body+∑c=1ncΔρc𝐠c,

where 𝐠body and 𝐠c are the measurements of a unit density in the whole body and in component c (prob.gbody, prob.G). The unknowns 𝐱=(ρbg,Δρ1,…,Δρnc) minimize

\lVertL−1(𝐲pred−𝐲)\rVert2+λ∑c(Δρcρ¯)2

subject to

  • the mass constraint ρbgV+∑cΔρcVc=M, with Vc the volume of component c inside the body and M = obs.mass_kg;
  • the bounds 0≤ρbg≤ρmax and 0≤ρbg+Δρc≤ρmax for every component, with ρmax = opts.rho_max_kgm3;
  • fixed parameters: with opts.background = "bulk" the background is held at the bulk density ρ¯=M/V; components with component.estimate_density false keep their relative density.

λ is the Tikhonov parameter opts.regularization. The problem is solved with lsqlin, first with the active-set algorithm and, if that does not converge, with the interior-point algorithm; if neither converges the run stops with sbtk:invert:solver.

Estimated geometry#

Besides the densities, an inversion can estimate the geometry of components. The geometry parameters are listed by sbtk.internal.geometry_parameters:

Field of the component Components Parameters
component.estimate_position = true sphere, ellipsoid, torus the three center coordinates, km (<name>_x, _y, _z)
component.estimate_position = [false false true] sphere, ellipsoid, torus only the coordinates of the mask, for example the height of a torus
component.estimate_axis = true torus the direction of its axis: two tilts about its own first and second axes, deg (<name>_tilt1, _tilt2)
component.estimate_axis = true ellipsoid its orientation: the two tilts of its third axis and the turn about it, deg (<name>_tilt1, _tilt2, _turn)

Setting either field on a component without a center or an axis stops the inversion with sbtk:invert:geometryParameter. The geometry is found by Gauss–Newton iteration:

  • Each step linearizes the measurements in the geometry parameters and solves the bounded problem. The derivatives are central differences of the integrals: 10⁻⁶ km for a sphere inside the body (a point mass), 10⁻⁴ km and 10⁻² deg for components integrated along rays, whose integrals are smooth only on scales larger than the ray spacing (Assumptions and limitations).
  • Trust region. The steps are limited to opts.step_km for a center coordinate and opts.step_deg for a tilt or turn. A step that does not lower the objective is undone and the trust region halved; a successful step restores it.
  • A priori constraints. With opts.position_sigma_km or opts.axis_sigma_deg finite, each center coordinate, tilt or turn has an a priori constraint of that 1σ about its starting value. These are needed when the measurements do not determine all of the geometry, and they keep a component from absorbing structure the model lacks (below).
  • Hard limits. opts.max_shift_km bounds the distance of an estimated center from its start, opts.max_tilt_deg the angle of an estimated axis from its starting direction, and opts.max_turn_deg the turn of an ellipsoid about its axis. Spheres are always kept inside the body.
  • Stopping. Iteration stops after opts.max_iter steps, or earlier when any of these holds:
  • the objective changes by less than 10⁻¹⁰ relative;
  • an accepted step changes every parameter by less than opts.geometry_tol of its step limit;
  • the trust region falls below 10⁻⁶ km.

Without the step test, a model that lacks structure the data contain keeps lowering χ2 by ever smaller steps. That runs every repetition about the center of mass to its limit.

For data about the center of mass the fit is repeated about the model's own center of mass (below), and each repetition continues from the geometry of the previous one. The priors and limits always refer to the geometry the components were given.

Absorbed structure. An estimated geometry can absorb structure the model lacks, so freeing it can lower χ2 while moving the component away from the truth. Example: a Didymos true model has a torus about its spin axis at the center of figure, plus a boulder and a random density field. The data are its exact values weighted by the Hera radio-science precision. An inversion model with a core, the torus and the regolith has a reduced χ2 of 121 (R2=−5.3) with fixed geometry. With the torus axis and height estimated (a priori 1σ of 1° and 10 m, limits of 10° and 50 m), χ2 drops to 39 while R2 falls to −5.7. The torus tilts 5.6° and moves 41 m up to stand in for the boulder. At this precision such priors are weak. Priors, or limits tight enough to bind, must express how well the geometry is actually known.

Local minima. A fit whose geometry absorbs structure can have more than one local minimum. The same Didymos fit, with the derivatives taken over smaller steps, settled with the torus 47 m below the center of figure and a reduced χ2 of 37; which minimum Gauss–Newton reaches depends on its path. Compare fits started from different geometries before reading a position or an axis as a result.

sbtk.interior.align_with_spin_axis is the counterpart for making a true model: it sets the axis of tori, ellipsoids or sectors along the model's own axis of the largest moment by fixed-point iteration (Density distributions).

Uncertainties#

The covariance of the parameters is the linearized one at the solution, with the mass constraint and the fixed parameters eliminated:

P=Z(Z𝖳J𝖳JZ)−1Z𝖳,

where J is the whitened Jacobian of the measurements with the regularization and a priori rows appended, and the columns of Z span the null space of the mass constraint and the fixed parameters. If Z𝖳J𝖳JZ is singular (the measurements do not determine every free parameter), the pseudo-inverse is used and fit.determined is false. The bounds are not included in P; fit.at_bound marks densities at a bound.

The density of a component and its 1σ are ρbg+Δρc and Pbg,bg+Pcc+2Pbg,c (fit.rho_kgm3, fit.rho_sigma_kgm3). fit.resolved marks components whose relative density exceeds its 1σ. The validation tests check over 40 noise realizations that the standard deviation of (estimate − truth)/σ is within 0.25 of 1, with diagonal and with strongly correlated covariances (Validation).

Regularization#

Models with many components, such as a sector grid, or weak data need Tikhonov regularization to keep noise from producing large alternating densities. sbtk.invert.choose_regularization returns the largest λ for which

χ2≤max(n, χmin2+2n),

with n the number of measurements and χmin2 the value at λ=10−2 (the discrepancy principle): χ2 may rise by about one standard deviation of its distribution. It searches log10λ∈[−2,8] by bisection with 9 solves; the result is returned, not stored, so set prob.opts.regularization before the final run.

Data about the center of mass#

When obs.coef_about is 'center_of_mass', the coefficients of degree 2 and higher are about the body's center of mass, which is known only through its measurement (the degree-1 rows). Expanding the model about the measured center of mass would carry the error of that measurement into the predictions: a translation of the expansion point changes the coefficients of degree l by terms proportional to those of lower degrees. sbtk.invert.run therefore

  1. keeps the model where it is: its geometry is built about the measured center of mass (fit.origin_km), from which layers and sectors are measured;
  2. moves its predicted coefficients of degree ≥ 2 and inertia to the model's own center of mass, by the exact translation of solid harmonics (sbtk.internal.sh_translation) and the parallel-axis theorem;
  3. iterates (Gauss–Newton, including the dependence of the center of mass on the densities, prob.D) until that center moves by less than 1 mm (fit.frame_iterations, fit.frame_offset_km);
  4. compares the model's center of mass with the measured one through the degree-1 rows.

fit.com_shift_km is the model's center of mass minus fit.origin_km. The tests testCenterOfMassFrameMatchesTheTrueFrame and testPredictionsAboutTheModelCenterOfMass check that the densities agree with an inversion about the true center of mass to within 0.2σ and that the predictions equal a forward model computed from scratch about the fitted center of mass (Validation).

Settings#

Setting (opts) Standard value Meaning
opts.moi_labels {'Ixx','Iyy','Izz'} Inertia rows fitted; {} for gravity coefficients only.
opts.regularization 0 Tikhonov parameter λ.
opts.background "estimate" "bulk" holds the background at M/V.
opts.rho_max_kgm3 4500 Upper bound on every density, kg/m³.
opts.max_iter 20 Gauss–Newton iterations for estimated geometry.
opts.step_km 0.010 Trust-region radius of a center coordinate, km.
opts.step_deg 1 Trust-region radius of an axis tilt or turn, deg.
opts.position_sigma_km Inf A priori 1σ of center coordinates, km.
opts.axis_sigma_deg Inf A priori 1σ of axis tilts and turns, deg.
opts.max_shift_km Inf Largest distance of an estimated center from its start, km.
opts.max_tilt_deg Inf Largest angle of an estimated axis from its start, deg.
opts.max_turn_deg Inf Largest turn of an estimated ellipsoid about its axis from its start, deg.
opts.geometry_tol 10⁻³ Converged when every geometry step is below this fraction of its step limit.

sbtk.invert.options(Name=Value) changes any of them; the fields can also be set afterwards.

Example#

MATLAB script: Estimation with several settings
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
cof = body.centroid_km;                                                % positions from the center of figure
true_components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof + [0.03 -0.02 0.01], 0.17, +500), ...
                   sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0.015, -500), ...
                   sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
true_components(2).center_km = cof;                                    % the torus about the z-axis through cof
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(true_components), 4, "estimation");
obs = sbtk.data.add_noise(sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc), 1);

components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", cof, 0.17, 0), ...         % geometry fixed, densities estimated
              sbtk.interior.torus("torus", 0.37, 0.055, 0, 0), ...
              sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, 0)];
components(2).center_km = cof;
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
hom  = sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob);                                  % is structure required?
fit  = sbtk.invert.run(prob);
sbtk.invert.summary(fit)

moving = components;  moving(1).estimate_position = true;              % estimate the core center as well
fit_p  = sbtk.invert.solve(body, moving, obs);
fprintf("core center [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m from the center of figure +- [%.0f %.0f %.0f] m\n", ...
        1e3*(fit_p.components(1).center_km - cof), 1e3*fit_p.center_sigma_km(1, :))

raised = components;  raised(2).estimate_position = [false false true];  % estimate the height of the torus
fit_z  = sbtk.invert.solve(body, raised, obs, sbtk.invert.options(max_shift_km=0.030));
fprintf("torus height %.1f m +- %.1f m (true 15 m)\n", 1e3*(fit_z.components(2).center_km(3) - cof(3)), 1e3*fit_z.center_sigma_km(2, 3))

The true core is at (30, −20, 10) m from the center of figure and the true torus 15 m above it; the fixed-geometry fit places both at the center of figure. More examples: Calculations.

Measurements and inversion

Goodness of fit and model comparison#

Chi-square test#

For a fit with residuals 𝐫=𝐲pred−𝐲 and measurement covariance Σ:

Quantity Definition Field
χ2 𝐫𝖳Σ−1𝐫, with the full covariance fit.chi2
Effective number of parameters peff=tr(JdPJd𝖳), the trace of the data resolution matrix (Jd whitened measurement Jacobian, P parameter covariance); it accounts for fixed parameters and regularization
Degrees of freedom ν=n−peff fit.dof
Reduced χ2 χ2/ν; close to 1 when the model and the stated uncertainties are correct fit.chi2_reduced
p-value P(χν2≥χ2), the probability that a correct model gives a χ2 at least as large, computed as the upper regularized incomplete gamma function Q(ν/2,χ2/2) fit.p_value
Consistent p≥0.05: the model is consistent with the measurements at the 5% significance level fit.consistent

sbtk.invert.goodness_of_fit computes the last three from χ2 and ν. When ν≤10−6 (at least as many parameters as measurements) the test is undefined: the reduced χ2 and the p-value are NaN and consistent is false.

Homogeneous body#

sbtk.invert.homogeneous fits a body of uniform density M/V to the same measurements; it has no free parameters (ν=n). If this fit is already consistent with the measurements, the data do not require internal structure at their precision.

Normalized residuals#

(ypred−y)/σ for every measurement (fit.normalized_residual, sbtk.plot.residuals). For a correct model about 68% lie within ±1. Large residuals concentrated in one group indicate structure that the model lacks: in the degree-1 rows, a model that cannot place the center of mass; at one degree, structure at the corresponding scale.

When a fit is rejected (p<0.05), its densities and uncertainties describe the best model of the chosen form, not the body. At high measurement precision, small structures that a component model omits, such as a random density field of a few percent of the bulk density or a boulder tens of meters across, can be enough to reject an otherwise correct model (Hera blind test).

Comparison with a true model#

In synthetic tests the true model is known. sbtk.compare.with_truth(body, truth, fit) evaluates both densities at the centroids of 24 radial shells of every facet cone (1,179,648 points for the 49,152-facet Didymos model), each weighted by the shell volume wi, with each model's layers and sectors measured from its own origin. It returns (cmp):

R2=1−∑iwi(ρest,i−ρtrue,i)2∑iwi(ρtrue,i−ρ¯true)2,

the fraction of the volume-weighted variance of the true density about its mean that the estimate explains: 1 for an exact estimate, 0 for one no better than a uniform density, negative for a worse one.

  • Rmax2: the largest R2 attainable with the same components, from a weighted least-squares fit of the true density by the background and the components. It measures the limit set by the choice of components; R2 close to Rmax2 means the measurements determined the densities as well as that geometry allows.
  • The volume-weighted RMS error and the standard deviation of the true density.
  • For each component present in both models: estimate, 1σ, true density and |estimate−true|/σ.

For many fits of the same components against one true model, sbtk.compare.reference samples the true model once and sbtk.compare.evaluate compares each fit in milliseconds. sbtk.compare.summary prints a comparison and sbtk.plot.comparison plots it.

Comparison of density grids#

Any two models can be compared on a common cubic grid, independently of how they are parametrized. sbtk.exchange.density_grid(body, model, spacing_km) evaluates a model at cell centers that lie at integer multiples of the spacing along the axes of the shape-model frame; cells whose center is inside the shape model (tested along rays from the center of figure) are kept, so all models of a body have the same cells (grid). sbtk.compare.grids(truth, estimate) compares the cells present in both grids (gridcmp): R2 with equal weights, RMS and mean error, and the fraction of cells whose error is at most twice the 1σ of the estimate. Both grids must have the same spacing (sbtk:compare:gridSpacing). This is how solutions in exchange packages are compared with interior-model packages.

Calibration of the uncertainties#

The uncertainties of a fit can be checked with repeated noise realizations: if they are correct, the standard deviation of (ρ^−ρtrue)/σ over many realizations is close to 1.

MATLAB script: Calibration over noise realizations
run("/path/to/SBTK/sbtk_setup.m")
body = sbtk.body.from_mass("Didymos", sbtk.shape.bundled("didymos"), 5.273e11, 0.43);
unc  = sbtk.data.uncertainties([sbtk.units.offset_to_degree1(0.002, 0.43), 1e-4, 2e-4, 4e-4], 2e-3, 0.02);
components = [sbtk.interior.sphere("core", body.centroid_km, 0.17, +450), sbtk.interior.layer("regolith", 0, 0.012, -900)];
[exact, truth] = sbtk.data.simulate(body, sbtk.interior.create(components), 4, "calibration");
exact = sbtk.data.set_uncertainties(exact, unc);

prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 1), sbtk.invert.options());
z = zeros(30, 3);
for k = 1:30
    f = sbtk.invert.run(sbtk.invert.replace_data(prob, sbtk.data.add_noise(exact, 100 + k)));
    z(k, :) = ([f.rho_bg_kgm3, [f.components.drho_kgm3]] - [truth.rho_bg_kgm3, [components.drho_kgm3]]) ...
              ./[f.rho_bg_sigma_kgm3, f.drho_sigma_kgm3];
end
fprintf("standard deviation of (estimate - truth)/sigma: %.2f\n", std(z(:)))

Files

Results folders and figures#

Run folders#

sbtk.io.new_run(project, name) creates the folder results/<project>/<yyyy-mm-dd_HHMMSS>_<name>/ in the repository and starts recording everything printed in the Command Window to log.txt in it, until sbtk.io.finish_run closes the log. It returns an out structure, which every save and report function takes. A new run never overwrites an earlier one.

  • sbtk.io.latest_run(project, name) returns the newest folder whose name after the time stamp equals name exactly: "didymos_T1" does not match didymos_T1_inversion. Inversion scripts use it to find the newest simulation.
  • sbtk.io.subfolder(out, name) makes the save and report functions write into a subfolder while the log stays in the run folder. The Hera simulation runners use it to keep the true model apart from the data package (Hera blind test).
MATLAB
out = sbtk.io.new_run("my_project", "T1_inversion");     % results/my_project/<date_time>_T1_inversion/
prob = sbtk.invert.setup(body, components, obs, sbtk.invert.options());
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, sbtk.invert.run(prob), sbtk.invert.homogeneous(prob));
sbtk.io.finish_run(out);

This fragment requires body, components and obs as defined in the first script.

Files#

File Written by Contents Read with
log.txt sbtk.io.new_run Everything printed during the run. a text editor
settings.json sbtk.io.save_settings, called by the report functions Body, degree, uncertainties, components, random field, noise seed and inversion settings of the run. jsondecode(fileread(file))
measurements.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_measurements The measurement set (obs); the text has only the diagonal of the coefficient covariance. sbtk.io.load_measurements
truth.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_truth The true model of a simulation (truth). sbtk.io.load_truth
fit.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_fit Densities with 1σ, χ2 test, every residual (fit). sbtk.io.load_fit
homogeneous.txt sbtk.io.report_inversion The same data fitted by a homogeneous body.
comparison.txt, .mat sbtk.io.save_comparison R2, Rmax2, RMS error, per-component comparison (cmp). load
figures/*.png sbtk.io.save_figure (200 dpi) The figures below.

The report functions write a standard set in one call:

Function Writes
sbtk.io.report_simulation(out, body, obs, truth) measurements.*, truth.*, settings.json, figures/truth_3d.png, truth_slices.png, measurements.png
sbtk.io.report_inversion(out, body, fit, homogeneous) fit.*, homogeneous.txt, settings.json, figures/residuals.png, densities.png, estimate_3d.png, estimate_slices.png
sbtk.io.report_comparison(out, body, truth, fit, cmp) comparison.*, settings.json, figures/comparison.png, truth_vs_estimate.png

Text formats#

Measurements (sbtk.io.write_measurements, sbtk.io.read_measurements): one keyword per line, values separated by spaces, # lines are comments. coef lines hold l, m, C¯lm, S¯lm and their 1σ; inertia lines hold the label, value, 1σ and the six weights. The first lines of a file:

Output

# inertia = one moment-of-inertia measurement on I/(M R_ref^2): label, value, 1-sigma, then

True models (sbtk.io.write_truth) and comparisons (sbtk.io.write_comparison) use the same layout.

Figures#

Every plot function returns a figure handle. sbtk.io.save_figure(out, fig, name) saves it as figures/<name>.png at 200 dpi in a run folder; exportgraphics saves it anywhere. Densities are drawn with a sequential color map (dark blue to yellow); signed differences with blue for lower and red for higher density.

The figures below come from one synthetic Didymos run, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m: a core (+450 kg/m³) at the center of figure, an equatorial torus (−500) about the z-axis through it, a 12 m regolith layer (−900), a boulder of radius 40 m (+900) and a random field of 40 kg/m³ with a 60 m correlation length; measurements to degree 4 with the uncertainties of the first script; an inversion for core, torus and regolith (the boulder and the field are not in the inversion model). The fit has χ2/ν=1.08 (p=0.36), the homogeneous body χ2/ν=45.0; R2=0.93 with Rmax2=0.98.

Shape model#

sbtk.plot.shape(body): the mesh with its center of figure and axes.

Interior in three dimensions#

sbtk.plot.interior3d(body, model, title): the surface drawn translucent; spheres, ellipsoids and tori drawn where they lie inside the body, layers by their lower boundary; color is the relative density. Sectors are not drawn (use slices). Saved as truth_3d.png and estimate_3d.png by the report functions.

Density slices#

sbtk.plot.slices(body, {models}, {titles}): the density on the plane z=0 (left) and the plane y=0 (right), both through the first model's origin, one row per model with a common color scale. Saved as truth_slices.png and estimate_slices.png.

Measurements#

sbtk.plot.measurements(obs): left, the root-mean-square size of the coefficients of each degree (points) and of their 1σ uncertainties (line); degrees where the points lie well above the line carry information about the interior. Degree 1 is close to zero about the center of mass. Right, each inertia measurement with its 1σ. Saved as measurements.png.

Normalized residuals#

sbtk.plot.residuals(fit): (predicted − measured)/σ for every measurement; gray band ±1σ, dashed lines ±2σ. Saved as residuals.png.

Estimated densities#

sbtk.plot.densities(fit): the density of the background and each component with its ±1σ interval; the dashed line is the background. Components whose relative density is smaller than its 1σ are drawn in gray. Saved as densities.png.

Comparison with the true model#

sbtk.plot.comparison(cmp): left, R2 of the estimate and Rmax2; right, each component's estimate with ±1σ and its true density (cross). Saved as comparison.png.

sbtk.plot.truth_vs_estimate(body, truth, fit): rows for the true density, the estimate (same color scale) and their difference, on the two planes through the true center of mass. Saved as truth_vs_estimate.png.

Difference from the homogeneous body#

sbtk.plot.difference_from_homogeneous(body, sets, names, scale, frame): for each set of gravity coefficients (a measurement set, a true model or an inversion result), the coefficients minus those of the homogeneous body (density M/V), both about their own center of mass, as radio-science fields are. Degree 1 shows the set's center of mass minus the center of figure. A measurement set about another point (for example a field about the shape-model origin) is first moved to its center of mass by the exact translation of solid harmonics. Zonal coefficients are shown as Jl=−C¯l0. With scale = "linear" the signed difference has ±3σ bars for sets with uncertainties; with "log" the absolute difference is drawn with 3σ as a separate line, which shows which departures from a uniform density the measurements resolve. With frame = "shape" both fields are in the shape-model axes; with "spin" in the spin axes of the set (z along its axis of the largest moment), where the set's C¯21, S¯21 vanish; with "principal" in its principal axes, where also S¯22 vanishes. The differences in the vanishing terms are the homogeneous body's own terms in those axes: they measure how far the principal axes of the interior are tilted and turned from those of the homogeneous body (Frames of a gravity field). Not saved by the report functions; save it with sbtk.io.save_figure.

Files

Exchange packages#

Exchange packages carry measurements, interior models and solutions between teams, for example in a blind test where one team simulates measurements of an interior it keeps hidden and other teams invert them. They are plain text with the units, frame and normalization written in them, and can be read without SBTK.

Package Name Written by Contents Released
Measurements <team>-DATA<n>-<comment> sbtk.exchange.write_data Gravity field, covariance, center of mass, moments of inertia, shape model with the data set
Interior model <team>-MOD<n>-<comment> sbtk.exchange.write_model True model, density grid, noise-free measurements, figures after the solutions
Solution <team>-SOL_<data team><n> sbtk.exchange.write_solution Estimated densities, covariance, fitted measurements, density grid, figures with the solution

sbtk.exchange.solution_name forms solution names; sbtk.exchange.locate finds the package of a given kind in a run folder and its redacted/ and unredacted/ subfolders.

File layout#

Each file starts with metadata lines # key: value, followed by one line of column names and comma-separated rows. Every column and key with a unit ends with it; NaN marks a value that is not provided.

Reader Statement
MATLAB T = readtable('gravity_field.txt', 'FileType', 'text', 'CommentStyle', '#');
Python with pandas T = pandas.read_csv('gravity_field.txt', comment='#')
Python, standard library rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in open('gravity_field.txt') if not l.startswith('#')))
SBTK sbtk.exchange.read_data(folder), sbtk.exchange.read_grid(file)

Measurement package#

File Contents
README.txt Summary (GM and mass, bulk density, degree and reference radius of the field; the uncertainties and the noise when the values have them) and the list of files.
gravity_field.txt l,m,C,S for degrees 2 and higher, fully normalized, about the center of mass, with sigma_C,sigma_S when the values have uncertainties.
gravity_covariance.txt Full covariance of those coefficients; rows and columns labeled. Only when the values have uncertainties.
center_of_mass.txt Center of mass in the shape-model frame (with its 3 × 3 covariance when it has one) and the center of figure.
moments_of_inertia.txt quantity,value,unit (and sigma): inertia elements as I/(MRref2) about the center of mass and/or the libration ratio. The sign convention of the products of inertia and the definition of the libration ratio are given when the file has them.
conventions.txt Units; the frame (what its origin and axes are, and the change of frame from the original shape-model file); the normalization, with MATLAB and Python code; degree 1 and the center of mass.
<shape>.obj The shape model the data were made with, in km, in the frame of every position of the package (The shape model of a package).

The gravity field is expanded about the center of mass, as a radio-science solution is, so it has no degree-1 terms; the position of the center of mass is a separate measurement in center_of_mass.txt. The package contains nothing about the interior: not the expansion origin of the simulation (the true center of mass), the noise seed, the model name or any component; testNothingAboutTheInterior checks this (Validation).

sbtk.exchange.read_data returns the measurement set with coef_about = 'center_of_mass': the coefficients of degree ≥ 2 with their covariance, degree-1 coefficients 0 ± σ that carry the uncertainty of the center of mass, the inertia rows, and the body built from the package's shape model and GM. A libration ratio becomes the row (B−A)−kIzz=0 with σ = σkIzz, using the measured Izz if the package has one and that of a homogeneous body otherwise.

The files state only what applies to the package. Those of a measurement package with uncertainties and noise, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

The shape model of a package#

A package's shape model is the one the data were made with, in the frame of every position of the package. A maker who changes the frame, as the HLP6 makers do (Frames of a gravity field), sends the original shape model moved and rotated into the new frame with sbtk.body.to_frame: every vertex becomes x′=(x−c)A, with c the center of mass of the true model and the columns of A the new axes, both in the frame of the original file. The shape itself does not change, only its coordinates.

Body Shape model of the package Origin Axes
Didymos CUB-DATA3-Didymos_didymos_v003_com_spin_axes.obj center of mass spin axes: z the axis of the largest moment, x the DART x-axis projected onto the plane normal to z
Dimorphos CUB-DATA6-Dimorphos_dimorphos_v004_com_principal_axes.obj center of mass principal axes: x the axis of the smallest and z of the largest moment

Each true model has its own center of mass and axes, so each package has its own shape model, and its file name starts with the name of the package: <package>_<shape name>.obj (sbtk.internal.shape_file_name). The interior-model package of the data set and a solution of it use the same name. A shape model taken unchanged from a file keeps the file's name.

The center of mass is then at the origin (to rounding), and the center of figure at −(rCoM−rCoF)A. The gravity field, the moments of inertia and center_of_mass.txt, and in the interior-model package every component and the density grid, are in this frame, so a receiving team uses the shape model as it is, with nothing to move or rotate. conventions.txt states what the origin and the axes are and the change of frame (o=c and A), so the coordinates of the original file are x=x′AT+c.

Packages of exact values#

A set without any uncertainties, such as the exact values of a true model (sbtk.data.simulate), is written as a package of exact values:

  • gravity_field.txt has the columns l,m,C,S, center_of_mass.txt the columns axis,center_of_mass_km,center_of_figure_km, and moments_of_inertia.txt the columns quantity,value,unit;
  • there is no gravity_covariance.txt;
  • neither the metadata nor the README has an uncertainties or noise line.

A maker's package of exact values in the frame with the center of mass as origin and the spin axes, made by documentation/tools/make_samples.m:

In a blind test the makers send such packages, and each receiving team applies uncertainties of its own choosing. sbtk.exchange.read_data reads them with NaN uncertainties. The inversion then stops with sbtk:data:noUncertainties until uncertainties are given, for example with sbtk.data.use_uncertainties from a precision file and sbtk.data.set_moi_sigma, after truncating with sbtk.data.select_degree to the degrees the precision covers. A set with some uncertainties but not all is not written (sbtk:data:noUncertainties).

Interior-model package#

File Contents
README.txt Summary (mass, bulk and background density, number of components, random field, density grid) and the list of files.
interior_model.txt name,type,relative_density_kgm3,density_kgm3,geometry for the background and every component; metadata: mass, bulk and background density, the point layers and sectors are measured from, the random field, the principal axes of inertia (unit vectors in the shape-model axes) and the principal moments A≤B≤C (Frames of a gravity field).
density_grid.txt x_km,y_km,z_km,density_kgm3,density_sigma_kgm3: the true density at the cell centers (σ = 0), random field included.
noise_free_data/ The measurement files without noise.
figures/ true_density_3d.png, true_density_slices.png.
Output
